passage:
Monday, week one. Jagdish, who managed the content team at a small Pune publisher, noticed that Preeti had missed another soft deadline, the third this month. Her chapter summaries came in late on Friday nights, and they were the best on the team. He caught himself drafting a message: "Please be more disciplined." He deleted it.
Wednesday, week two. He asked her to walk with him to the chai stall. "Your work is excellent. The late part puzzles me. What makes these tasks hard to start?"
Preeti was quiet a long moment. "Honestly? I'm never sure what length you want. And after the sales team called my first draft 'amateur' in March, I rewrite everything five times before anyone sees it."
Friday, week three. Jagdish now sent a one-line scope with every brief and a mid-week note: "Send me a rough draft. Rough is fine."
Preeti's summary arrived on Thursday afternoon.

qa.q: How many soft deadlines had Preeti missed that month by week one?
qa.a: She had missed the third soft deadline this month.

qa.q: What fear or worry was really making Preeti delay?
qa.a: She was unsure what length was wanted and still afraid of being called 'amateur', so she rewrote everything five times before showing anyone.

qa.q: Which changes did Jagdish make, and why did they work?
qa.a: He added a one-line scope and a mid-week request for a rough draft, which cleared the unclear scope and eased her fear of judgement.

qa.q: How might Preeti have felt when Jagdish asked what made the tasks hard?
qa.a: She may have felt relieved and respected, since he asked instead of judging her character, which made it safe to admit the fear.

grounding: Shows a manager who notices a capable employee's late but strong work and, by asking what makes tasks hard, uncovers unclear scope and fear.

passage:
Nikita, you said your new analyst keeps sending things at the last minute, and you're ready to write "lacks discipline" in his review. Your Gautam uncle made that exact mistake once.
The first team I led, at twenty-six, was in a bank in Kochi. There was a young man, Suresh, bright as anything. Every report late, every report excellent. I decided he was careless, and one day I said so in front of the team. He went red and said nothing. Things got worse.
Months later, over lunch, I finally asked, "What makes these reports hard for you?" It all came out. He was doing his own work and covering for a colleague on leave, and nobody had told him which reports came first. He was drowning and too proud to say it. I felt terrible.
So before you write that review, Nikita, ask him one question. Not "Why are you late?" but "What makes this hard?"

qa.q: Where did Gautam lead a team at twenty-six?
qa.a: In a bank in Kochi.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel after learning why Suresh was late?
qa.a: He felt terrible, realising Suresh had been drowning in work and unclear priorities, not being careless.

qa.q: What does Gautam advise Nikita to do before writing the review?
qa.a: Ask the analyst 'What makes this hard?' instead of judging his discipline, since the answer may reveal overload, unclear scope or fear.

qa.q: What might Suresh have felt when Gautam called him careless in front of the team?
qa.a: Suresh likely felt humiliated and unseen, already overloaded and too proud to explain, which is why he went red and said nothing.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a manager who judged a late but capable employee's character before asking and finding overload and unclear priorities.

passage:
It was quarter-end, the office was stretched thin, and Anjali had three reports due on her own desk. Still, she'd noticed a pattern with Maria. Maria missed every soft deadline, drafts by Tuesday, outline by Thursday, and then, at the very last minute, handed in work that was genuinely excellent.
Anjali's first thought was, she's just disorganised. But she stopped herself. Maria wasn't careless. So what was going on?
On Friday, with ten minutes between calls, she asked, "Maria, what makes these reports hard to start?"
Maria looked surprised. Then she said, "Honestly? I'm never sure what you want. I'm scared of getting the scope wrong."

qa.q: What did Maria say she was scared of?
qa.a: Getting the scope wrong.

qa.q: What was Anjali thinking when she stopped herself?
qa.a: She felt curious and cautious, not wanting to judge Maria as disorganised when the work was so good.

qa.q: Why was Anjali's question useful at this stage?
qa.a: It revealed the real issue, fear and unclear scope, which clearer briefs can fix.

qa.q: What is it like for Maria to be asked this question?
qa.a: Maria seems surprised and perhaps relieved to be asked rather than blamed.

grounding: Shows a manager noticing a capable employee's late starts and asking what makes the task hard, which reveals fear and unclear scope.

passage:
Gargi had managed Vinita for a year in the Bengaluru office. Vinita's final presentations were the best on the team. But she missed every draft deadline, and Gargi had started to feel irritated.
In her head, the word "lazy" kept coming up. She didn't like that.
So on Wednesday she took Vinita for coffee. "I want to understand something. Your final work is great, but the drafts always come late. What makes the early stages hard?"
Vinita stared at her cup. "I have four projects. I don't know which one matters most. So I freeze and do them all at the end."
Gargi nodded slowly. It wasn't laziness. It was overload.

qa.q: How long had Gargi managed Vinita?
qa.a: A year.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling as the word "lazy" kept coming up?
qa.a: She felt irritated and uncomfortable with her own judgement, which is why she decided to ask instead.

qa.q: What did Gargi's question reveal, and what could she do next?
qa.a: It revealed overload across four projects; she could help Vinita set priorities or reduce the load.

qa.q: What is it like for Vinita to explain her freezing?
qa.a: Vinita seems relieved but embarrassed, admitting she freezes because she doesn't know what matters most.

grounding: Shows a manager curious rather than judgemental about a strong employee's missed drafts, discovering overload behind the delays.

passage:
"Preeti, got a minute?"
"Sure, Ujjwal. Is something wrong?"
"Not wrong. Your final analysis last week was brilliant."
"Thanks!"
"But the first draft was due Monday and came Thursday night. Same as the month before."
"I know. I'm sorry. I'm just bad at deadlines."
"I don't think it's that. What makes the start hard?"
Preeti hesitated. "If I send a draft and it's not good, you'll think I'm not good enough for this role."
"So you wait until it's perfect."
"Yes."
"Okay. What if drafts could be rough? I only want to check direction."

qa.q: When was the first draft due?
qa.a: On Monday.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal be feeling on saying "I don't think it's that"?
qa.a: Ujjwal seems curious and caring, not wanting to judge Preeti's character.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's question uncover, and what is the response?
qa.a: It uncovers fear of being judged; Ujjwal offers that drafts can be rough and only for direction.

qa.q: What is it like for Preeti to admit this fear?
qa.a: Preeti seems nervous and vulnerable, but perhaps relieved once it is said.

grounding: Shows a manager asking a capable employee what makes starting hard, instead of judging, which reveals fear of being judged.

passage: For three months I had Sumit filed under "brilliant but unreliable". His soft deadlines slid by a day or two, every time, and then at the last moment he'd send a report so good I forgave it. I was drafting a stern note about time management when I stopped and asked myself what I actually knew. Nothing, really. So I asked him for coffee instead. I said, "Your work is strong. What makes starting these reports hard?" He was quiet for a while. Then: "Bidisha, honestly, I never know how deep you want them. So I wait until I'm scared enough to just guess." I had been judging his character, and the problem was my vague brief. Now each report starts with a five-line scope from me. His last one came in two days early.

qa.q: How had Bidisha filed Sumit for three months?
qa.a: Under "brilliant but unreliable".

qa.q: Why did Bidisha stop drafting the stern note?
qa.a: Bidisha felt unsure and a little uneasy, realising the judgement rested on almost nothing Bidisha actually knew.

qa.q: What did asking instead of judging reveal, and what fixed it?
qa.a: It revealed an unclear scope, not a character flaw, and a five-line scope at the start fixed it.

qa.q: What had the vague briefs been like for Sumit?
qa.a: Sumit was anxious and unsure how deep to go, so he waited until fear pushed him to guess.

grounding: Shows a manager who, instead of judging a capable employee's late but strong work, asks what makes starting hard and finds unclear scope.
